analyst_observations: Highly discriminating evals this iteration: prohibitions-cbc-design (+50pp), cbc-sample-size-with-subgroups (+50pp), cross-wave-maxdiff-comparability (+50pp), anchoring-absolute-importance (+50pp), method-selection-maxdiff (+50pp). The skill is cleanly adding value on method-specific guard rails the base model misses.

Eval-7 (dual-response-none-cbc) was the weakest discriminator at +25pp. Base model disagrees with the PM and identifies the right risks, but defaults to treating dual-response and explicit None as equally valid rather than establishing dual-response as the default. Consider strengthening the eval assertion or prompt to force the distinction more cleanly.

Eval-3 (sparse-maxdiff-design) is the only eval where the with_skill response failed an assertion (individual-level degradation at k=75). The skill SKILL.md covers this, but the response framed the design constraints per-respondent rather than naming k=75 as a ceiling for individual-level readout. Consider adding a note to the SKILL.md trigger for this.

Without-skill pattern: base model correctly recommends the right method (MaxDiff, CBC, sparse design) in every case. The failure modes are: (a) missing anchoring guidance, (b) underpowered sample sizes with flat rules-of-thumb, (c) treating prohibitions as standard rather than a last resort, (d) recommending equating approximations instead of re-fielding with anchoring for cross-wave comparability.

Eval-5 (cross-wave-maxdiff-comparability) without-skill response is actively misleading — recommends z-score equating as a viable technique, which the skill correctly identifies as insufficient. This is the highest-risk gap in base model behavior.

Rate limiting during the run prevented timing/token data from being captured for most with_skill evals. Iteration-1 data suggests with_skill tokens are approximately 23-27k (vs. 12-14k without_skill), roughly 1.8-2x overhead for reference file reading.
